title: Aircraft, Marine & Railroad Transportation Equipment Wholesaling in the US
one_liner: A specialized B2B wholesale channel for aircraft parts, marine equipment and rail equipment, driven mostly by aerospace aftermarket demand.
overview: This industry wholesales transportation equipment and supplies excluding motor vehicles and marine pleasure craft, including aircraft engines and parts, commercial marine machinery and supplies, railroad cars, locomotives, rail equipment and related service receipts. The baseline IBIS file shows 2021 revenue of $56.3 billion and a 2021-2026 forecast CAGR of 2.9%, with aircraft-related goods representing the majority of revenue. Current 2025-2026 conditions are more uneven than the baseline recovery story: commercial aerospace backlogs and aftermarket parts demand are strong, freight rail equipment orders are cyclically weaker, and marine-related demand is supported more by Navy and Coast Guard shipbuilding than by recreational boating.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimated market size: about $63.1 billion, modeled from the baseline 2021 revenue of $56.3 billion and the baseline 2021-2026 CAGR of 2.9%.
key_stats.growth: 2025 modeled growth: about 2.9% year over year, consistent with the baseline 2021-2026 recovery forecast; 2026 growth risk is mixed because aerospace demand is strong while railcar orders and recreational marine sales weakened in 2025.
key_stats.establishments: 2023 Census Business Patterns reported 2,375 employer establishments for NAICS 423860.
key_stats.census_revenue_benchmark: 2022 Economic Census benchmark for NAICS 423860 was about $49.7 billion in sales, value of shipments or revenue.
key_stats.air_traffic: April 2026 U.S. air carrier revenue passenger enplanements were 80.8 million, nearly flat versus 80.8 million in April 2025, while revenue freight ton-miles rose to 755.5 million from 660.1 million.
key_stats.freight_index: April 2026 Freight Transportation Services Index was 139.6, versus 136.9 in December 2025.
key_stats.aircraft_deliveries: Boeing delivered 600 commercial aircraft in 2025, up 72% from 348 in 2024; Airbus delivered 793 commercial aircraft in 2025, up 4% from 766 in 2024.
key_stats.railcar_indicator: Trinity received orders for 5,155 railcars and delivered 9,500 railcars in 2025, down from 7,685 orders and 17,570 deliveries in 2024.
key_stats.marine_indicator: NMMA reported 2025 new boat retail unit sales of 215,237, down 8.8% from 236,070 in 2024.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 baseline estimate: about $57.9 billion, implied by the local IBIS baseline's 2021 revenue of $56.3 billion and 2021-2026 CAGR forecast of 2.9%.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 baseline growth: about 2.9%, using the local IBIS 2021-2026 forecast CAGR.
baseline_2022.profit_margin: 2021 baseline profit margin: 2.8% of revenue; 2026 baseline forecast profit margin: 5.7% of revenue.
baseline_2022.employment: 2021 baseline employment: 37,646 workers; 2026 baseline forecast employment: 42,506 workers.
baseline_2022.product_mix: 2021 baseline: aircraft equipment and supplies including engines and parts were 57.9% of revenue, marine machinery and supplies were 5.8%, service receipts were 1.0%, other transportation equipment was 14.9%, and aircraft-related products overall were described as 78.3% of revenue.

how_it_makes_money: Wholesalers buy aircraft, marine and rail equipment from OEMs, parts manufacturers, surplus channels and import sources, then resell inventory to airlines, aircraft MRO providers, defense customers, shipbuilders, railroads, leasing companies and industrial users. Revenue comes from parts markup, inventory availability, logistics, same-day or aircraft-on-ground fulfillment, kitting, vendor-managed inventory, used serviceable material, repairable exchange programs, and limited service/labor charges.
cost_structure: The model is inventory-heavy and margin-sensitive. The largest cost is purchased equipment and parts, followed by wages for technical sales, warehouse, quality and logistics staff; freight, warehousing and inventory carrying costs; IT and traceability systems; insurance and compliance; and rent near airports, ports, rail hubs and aerospace clusters. Profit is constrained by OEM channel power, surplus-parts competition, customer concentration in airlines and defense, and the need to hold expensive specialized inventory.
major_players: Boeing Global Services / Boeing Distribution Services
Trinity Industries rail products and parts
Greenbrier railcar manufacturing, parts and services
current_dynamics: Aerospace is the strongest leg of the market in 2025-2026. Boeing's 2025 commercial deliveries recovered sharply and Airbus ended 2025 with a record 8,754-aircraft backlog, extending demand for spares, consumables and MRO distribution. Airlines are flying high-utilization fleets while delayed new aircraft deliveries keep older aircraft in service longer, which supports used serviceable material and aftermarket replacement parts. Rail equipment is softer: Trinity's 2025 railcar orders and deliveries fell sharply from 2024, and industry commentary pointed to fleet rationalization and storage levels above 21% in 2025. Marine is bifurcated: recreational boating demand fell in 2025 under high-rate consumer pressure, but Navy and Coast Guard shipbuilding plans and maritime industrial-base funding support defense and commercial vessel supply chains.
whats_growing: Aircraft aftermarket distribution, AOG fulfillment, used serviceable material, OEM-authorized parts distribution, digital parts marketplaces, government and defense aviation support, Airbus and Boeing fleet material services, and shipbuilding-related marine components tied to U.S. naval investment are growing in 2025-2026.
whats_shrinking: New railcar equipment demand, discretionary recreational marine channels, low-value commodity parts distribution, independent distributors without OEM authorization or scale, and purely transactional wholesalers that cannot provide traceability, compliance, kitting or inventory-management services are shrinking or losing share.
recent_developments: 2026-01-12: Airbus reported 793 commercial aircraft deliveries in 2025, up 4% year over year, and a record year-end backlog of 8,754 aircraft.
2026-01-27: Boeing reported 600 commercial aircraft deliveries in 2025, up 72% from 2024, and total company backlog of $682 billion at December 31, 2025.
2026-03-11: NMMA reported full-year 2025 new boat retail unit sales of 215,237, down 8.8% from 2024.
2026-04-22: GAO testified that the FY2027 budget requested over $65 billion in shipbuilding funding, highlighting major demand but also capacity and execution challenges.
2026-07-01: FRED/BTS showed the Freight Transportation Services Index at 139.6 for April 2026, up from 136.9 in December 2025.
2026-07-16: AAR reported fiscal 2025 sales of $2.8 billion, up 20%, with new-parts distribution sales growing more than 20% organically in the fourth quarter.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is cautiously positive, with growth led by aerospace aftermarket and defense-related marine demand rather than a broad-based transportation equipment cycle. Aircraft delivery backlogs, aging fleets, MRO activity and government aviation support should keep parts distributors busy, but margins remain exposed to OEM channel control, inventory financing costs, quality traceability requirements and supply-chain bottlenecks. Rail equipment wholesalers face weaker replacement demand until carloads, lease rates and storage levels improve. Marine wholesalers tied to shipbuilding and defense programs should outperform those tied to recreational boating. A reasonable 2026 industry view is low-single-digit growth with stronger aerospace mix and continued consolidation pressure.

title: Alarm, Horn & Traffic Control Equipment Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: A mature electronics-manufacturing niche selling alarms, sirens, intercoms and traffic-control hardware into buildings, vehicles, factories and public infrastructure.
overview: This industry manufactures alarm systems, hazard-detection systems, traffic signals, sirens, horns, intercommunication systems and related control equipment. Demand is tied to nonresidential construction, manufacturing facilities, vehicle production and registrations, municipal road work, rail crossings and safety-code compliance. The 2022 baseline described a mature, low-concentration industry with high globalization, high import penetration and a shift by US producers toward higher-margin custom, integrated and software-enabled systems. Current 2025-2026 conditions are mixed: public highway and street construction remains elevated, federal safety funds continue through fiscal 2026, and connected traffic systems are growing, while private manufacturing construction spending fell through 2025 and into 2026 after a major 2022-2024 buildout.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimated revenue: about $4.8 billion, extrapolated from the 2022 IBISWorld baseline of $4.549 billion and its 2022-2027 forecast CAGR of 1.6%.
key_stats.growth: 2022-2027 forecast CAGR: 1.6%; 2025 demand was mixed as traffic infrastructure stayed firm but manufacturing construction weakened.
key_stats.imports: 2022 imports: $1.708 billion; 2022 imports equaled 29.7% of domestic demand; 2027 forecast import share: 29.1%.
key_stats.demand_indicators: 2024 US motor-vehicle registrations: 297.5 million; June 2026 public highway and street construction spending: $150.9 billion SAAR; June 2026 private manufacturing construction spending: $170.3 billion SAAR.

baseline_2022.growth: 2022 revenue growth: 2.1%; 2017-2022 revenue CAGR: -1.4%; 2022-2027 forecast revenue CAGR: 1.6%.
baseline_2022.product_mix: 2022 revenue mix: alarm systems 49.7%, vehicle and pedestrian traffic-control equipment 26.0%, intercommunication systems 22.4%, other 1.9%.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers sell finished and custom electronic safety products to OEMs, contractors, distributors, municipalities, transportation agencies, commercial-building integrators and industrial users. Revenue comes from factory-built alarm panels, fire and gas detection devices, sirens, horns, vehicle alarms, traffic signal controllers, cabinets, pedestrian signals, intercom systems, sensors, remote-control units and increasingly integrated hardware-software traffic and building-safety packages. Higher-margin work is concentrated in custom commercial, government, industrial and smart-traffic systems rather than commoditized standalone devices.
cost_structure: The 2022 baseline cost profile was electronics-heavy and labor-supported: profit was 6.5% of revenue, wages were $964 million or 21.2% of revenue, and the remaining cost base was mainly purchased electronic components, metal and plastic housings, semiconductors, sensors, circuit boards, compliance testing, freight, depreciation, rent, sales and engineering overhead. In 2025-2026, tariffs and supply-chain rules raised the strategic value of US assembly and Buy America-compliant production for traffic-control equipment, while imported components continued to pressure margins on basic alarms and intercoms.
major_players: Carrier legacy fire brands / Kidde-related assets now outside Carrier after the 2024 fire-business sale
current_dynamics: The traffic-control side is stronger than the broad electronics baseline because IIJA highway programs run through fiscal 2026 and public highway construction remained near $151 billion SAAR in June 2026. Municipal buyers are upgrading signal cabinets, adaptive controllers, pedestrian safety equipment, detection sensors and V2X-ready roadside infrastructure. Building alarm demand is steadier but more exposed to the mix of commercial construction, retrofit cycles and code-driven fire/life-safety replacement. Manufacturing-facility alarm demand cooled in 2025-2026 as private manufacturing construction spending fell from $240.9 billion SAAR in December 2024 to $170.3 billion SAAR in June 2026. Automotive horn and vehicle-alarm demand is supported by the 2024 registered vehicle base of 297.5 million, but OEM volumes and import competition limit upside for domestic manufacturers.
whats_growing: Adaptive traffic controllers, connected-intersection equipment, V2X-ready roadside units, cloud-managed traffic systems, cybersecurity-hardened traffic software, pedestrian safety signals, rail-crossing safety equipment, integrated fire/gas/security panels for industrial facilities, and Buy America-compliant traffic-control hardware are growing. Demand is also supported by 2025 HSIP funding of $3.177 billion and 2026 HSIP funding of $3.246 billion under the IIJA.
whats_shrinking: Commoditized standalone alarms, basic intercom systems, low-end vehicle alarms and products with high import substitutability are shrinking or losing share. The 2025-2026 decline in private manufacturing construction spending is a headwind for new-facility industrial alarm installations. The number of domestic establishments and enterprises is expected to keep edging down through 2027 as larger operators consolidate, offshore lower-value production, or focus on higher-spec systems.
recent_developments: 2025-02: Honeywell announced a plan to separate Automation and Aerospace, sharpening focus on building and industrial automation markets.
2025-08: Johnson Controls completed the sale of its residential and light commercial HVAC business to Bosch, continuing its shift toward commercial building solutions.
2025-09: Econolite announced a 50,000-square-foot San Diego production facility, its fourth US manufacturing site, to support Build America, Buy America demand.
2026-01: The White House announced Section 232 actions on semiconductor and derivative-product imports, adding supply-chain and tariff risk for electronics-heavy manufacturers.
2026-03: FHWA listed a MUTCD Revision 1 final rule among 2026 IIJA implementation updates, relevant to traffic-control equipment standards.
2026-06: FRED/Census data showed public highway and street construction at $150.9 billion SAAR and private manufacturing construction at $170.3 billion SAAR.
outlook: The industry should grow slowly rather than break out. Traffic-control equipment has the clearest 2025-2027 runway because federal highway, safety and smart-mobility programs are still flowing and agencies are modernizing intersections for pedestrian safety, analytics and connected vehicles. Alarm systems should remain resilient because fire and life-safety equipment is code-driven, but new commercial and manufacturing construction is less supportive than it was in 2022-2024. Import penetration, electronics tariffs, semiconductor availability and compliance with Buy America rules will decide whether domestic producers gain share or simply absorb higher costs. A reasonable 2025-2027 outlook is low-single-digit annual revenue growth with better margins for custom integrated systems and weaker economics for commodity devices.

title: Allergy Medicine Manufacturing OTC
one_liner: Manufacturers of nonprescription antihistamines, nasal corticosteroids and decongestants serve a large, recurring allergy-relief market shaped by pollen intensity, retail shelf competition, private label growth and FDA monograph changes.
overview: This industry manufactures over-the-counter allergy medicines sold without a prescription, including branded and generic antihistamines, intranasal corticosteroids, decongestants and combination allergy-relief products. Baseline IBIS data put 2021 revenue at $3.6B and projected revenue at $4.2B by 2026, driven by healthcare utilization, physician and pharmacist recommendations, R&D, price increases and steady allergy prevalence. Current 2025-2026 conditions are mixed: CDC 2024 data show 25.2% of US adults and 20.6% of children had seasonal allergies, while AAFA's 2025 Allergy Capitals report says climate change is making pollen seasons longer and more intense. At the same time, Bayer reported 2025 North American allergy weakness from a soft season, FDA actions are forcing label and formulation review, and private-label manufacturers such as Perrigo continue gaining share in upper respiratory products.

key_stats.market_size: 2026: about $4.2B US OTC allergy medicine manufacturing revenue, based on the baseline 2021-2026 IBIS projection in 2021 dollars.
key_stats.growth: 2021-2026: projected 3.1% CAGR in the baseline IBIS outlook; 2025 demand was uneven because Bayer reported a soft North American allergy season while Perrigo reported 2025 upper respiratory net sales up 5.8%.
key_stats.allergy_prevalence: 2024: 25.2% of US adults and 20.6% of US children had seasonal allergies, according to CDC/NCHS.
key_stats.otc_upper_respiratory_volume: 2025: US OTC upper respiratory medicine volume reached 1.223B units, up from 1.169B units in 2024 but below 1.317B units in 2022, according to CHPA/Statista.
key_stats.profit_margin: 2026: baseline IBIS outlook projected average industry EBIT margin of 6.8%, nearly flat with 2021's 6.7%.
key_stats.trade_exposure: 2026: baseline IBIS outlook projected imports of $2.5B and exports of $552.5M, reflecting high globalization and API/formulation outsourcing.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: about $3.7B estimated US OTC allergy medicine manufacturing revenue, derived from the baseline 2021 revenue of $3.623B and the 2021-2026 projected CAGR of 3.1%.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022: about 3.1% estimated annual revenue growth under the baseline IBIS projection path.
baseline_2022.product_mix: 2021 baseline mix: antihistamines 62.1% of revenue, corticosteroids 29.5%, decongestants and other 8.4%.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue by producing national-brand and store-brand OTC allergy medicines for retail pharmacies, mass merchants, grocery stores, club stores, e-commerce channels and wholesalers. Branded players monetize consumer trust, advertising, line extensions and premium formats such as 24-hour tablets, children's liquids, dissolvables and nasal sprays. Generic and private-label players monetize scale manufacturing, FDA-compliant equivalents and retailer economics that let stores price below national brands while preserving margins.

cost_structure.materials_and_packaging: 2025-2026: active pharmaceutical ingredients, excipients, bottles, blister packs, cartons and nasal-spray delivery components remain the largest operating cost category, with sourcing exposed to global API and packaging supply chains.
cost_structure.manufacturing_labor: 2026: baseline IBIS outlook projected wages of $735.7M, up from $638M in 2021, as quality, regulatory, R&D and technical labor costs rise.
cost_structure.marketing_and_trade_spend: 2025-2026: national brands rely on TV, digital media, coupons, retail promotions and seasonal shelf placement, while private-label competitors spend less on consumer advertising but compete for retailer programs.
cost_structure.r_and_d_and_regulatory: 2025-2026: costs include OTC monograph compliance, bioequivalence or switch work, stability testing, adverse-event monitoring, label updates and reformulation planning after FDA actions on phenylephrine and cetirizine/levocetirizine warnings.
cost_structure.profit: 2026: baseline IBIS outlook projected EBIT margin at 6.8%, with margins pressured by private-label competition, higher labor and compliance costs, and retailer bargaining power.

major_players: Kenvue: Zyrtec, Benadryl, Sudafed and Rhinocort brands in its Self Care segment; 2025 company net sales were $15.1B.
Bayer: Claritin and related allergy/cold products; 2025 Consumer Health sales were EUR 5.802B and Allergy & Cold sales were EUR 1.173B, down 6.3% reported.
Haleon: Flonase and broader consumer health portfolio after the 2022 GSK/Pfizer consumer health separation; 2025 annual report reflects a pure-play consumer health company.
Opella: Allegra, Xyzal and Nasacort following Sanofi's April 30, 2025 sale of a controlling Opella stake to CD&R, with Sanofi retaining 48.2%.

Perrigo: leading store-brand/private-label self-care manufacturer; 2025 Upper Respiratory net sales were $529.5M, up 5.8%, including allergy products comparable to Zyrtec, Claritin, Nasacort and Flonase.
current_dynamics: The category is being pulled in two directions in 2025-2026. Demand fundamentals are strong because allergies are common, pollen seasons are lengthening and self-care remains a durable consumer behavior. However, retail volume can swing with weather and pollen intensity, and Bayer specifically cited a soft 2025 allergy season in North America. Private label is structurally gaining because cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine, fluticasone and triamcinolone are widely available as generics. Regulatory scrutiny is also increasing: FDA's 2024 proposal to remove oral phenylephrine from the OTC monograph threatens combination allergy-decongestant products, while FDA's 2025 cetirizine/levocetirizine warning adds labeling and pharmacovigilance work for Zyrtec, Xyzal and generics.
whats_growing: Intranasal corticosteroids, 24-hour nonsedating antihistamines, children's allergy formats, e-commerce/omnichannel replenishment, HSA/FSA-eligible OTC purchasing, private-label equivalents and climate-linked seasonal demand are growing. Perrigo's 2025 upper respiratory sales increase and AAFA's 2025 findings on longer, more intense pollen seasons support continued demand for both branded and store-brand allergy relief.
whats_shrinking: Single-ingredient oral phenylephrine and phenylephrine-containing combination decongestant products are shrinking strategically because FDA proposed in November 2024 to remove oral phenylephrine as an OTC nasal decongestant active ingredient. Brand premiums are also under pressure where mature molecules face store-brand equivalents. 2025 was weaker for some branded seasonal products, with Bayer reporting a North American soft allergy season and a 6.3% reported decline in 2025 Allergy & Cold sales.
recent_developments: 2024-11-07: FDA proposed removing oral phenylephrine from the OTC monograph for nasal congestion after concluding it is not effective for that use.
2025-03-18: AAFA released its 2025 Allergy Capitals report, citing longer and more intense pollen seasons and ranking Wichita, Kansas as the top allergy capital for the third straight year.
2025-04-30: Sanofi closed the sale of a 50.0% controlling stake in Opella to CD&R, creating an independent consumer health company that includes Allegra, Xyzal and Nasacort.
2025-05-16: FDA required warnings about rare but severe itching after stopping long-term use of oral cetirizine or levocetirizine, affecting OTC and prescription forms such as Zyrtec and Xyzal.
2026-02-26: Perrigo reported 2025 Upper Respiratory net sales of $529.5M, up 5.8%, citing increased distribution of cough, cold and allergy products.
2026-05-26: CHPA/Statista reported 2025 US OTC upper respiratory medicine volume of 1.223B units, up from 1.169B units in 2024.
outlook: The 2026-2030 outlook is moderate-growth rather than breakout. Baseline industry revenue should remain near the 2026 projected $4.2B level and grow with pollen exposure, price/mix, nasal spray adoption and self-care behavior. Upside comes from longer allergy seasons, OTC switch activity, retailer support for private label and online replenishment. Downside comes from soft seasonal weather, aggressive store-brand pricing, FDA-driven reformulations, retailer power and consumers trading down. Manufacturers with broad molecule coverage, flexible packaging/formulation capacity and strong retailer relationships are best positioned.
themes: Regulatory reformulation risk from OTC monograph changes
Brand portfolios shifting after consumer health spinouts
Retailer bargaining power and omnichannel replenishment
Nasal corticosteroids and 24-hour antihistamines gaining mix
one_sentence: The US OTC allergy medicine manufacturing industry remains a mature but resilient consumer health category, with 2026 manufacturer revenue estimated near $4.2B as demand from seasonal allergies offsets generic price pressure and reformulation risk in oral decongestants.

title: Ambulance Manufacturing
one_liner: A small, consolidated specialty-vehicle industry that finishes ambulance bodies on purchased chassis for EMS agencies, hospitals, fire departments and private ambulance operators.
overview: Ambulance manufacturers build Type I, Type II, Type III and specialty emergency medical vehicles, typically by mounting or converting patient-care modules on purchased Ford, GM, Ram or other truck and van chassis. The 2022 baseline sized the US industry at $718.0 million, and its 2022 forecast implied a roughly flat-to-slightly-down path to 2027, but public 2025-2026 evidence points to unusually firm near-term order books because EMS agencies are still replacing older units delayed by pandemic-era chassis and component shortages. Demand is structurally supported by healthcare spending, Medicare/Medicaid reimbursement flows, local-government capital budgets and a fast-growing 65+ population, while profitability depends on chassis supply, steel/aluminum, electrical systems, HVAC, lighting, labor productivity and the ability to pass price increases through fixed municipal procurement cycles.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: about $712 million estimated US industry revenue in 2022 dollars, interpolated from the 2022 IBISWorld baseline forecast of $708.9 million for 2027
key_stats.growth: 2022-2027: -0.3% forecast CAGR in the baseline; 2025 public-company data showed higher shipments, price realization and backlog in ambulance-containing specialty-vehicle segments
key_stats.product_mix: 2022: Type I 47.1% of revenue, Type II 26.9%, Type III 23.7%, other ambulance types 2.3%
key_stats.imports_exports: 2022: $52.6 million imports and $44.9 million exports; Canada accounted for more than 99.0% of 2022 imports in the baseline
key_stats.demand_driver: 2025: US population age 65+ reached 64.6 million, up 16.2% from April 1, 2020

baseline_2022.growth: 2022: -6.4% expected annual revenue decline; 2017-2022 revenue CAGR: 0.8%

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue by designing, fabricating and assembling ambulances on purchased chassis, then selling completed units through direct sales teams, dealer networks, government procurement channels and fleet contracts. Additional revenue comes from custom specifications, remounts, refurbishment, parts, warranty work, service packages, module upgrades, connectivity systems and compliance-driven retrofits. Buyers include municipal EMS agencies, fire departments, hospitals, private ambulance operators and large multi-state fleet operators.

cost_structure.largest_costs: 2025: purchased chassis, ambulance modules, steel, aluminum, composites, electrical systems, HVAC, lighting, sirens, cabinetry, stretchers and medical-equipment integration remain the main cost base
cost_structure.labor: 2022: wages were $124.0 million, equal to about 17.3% of 2022 industry revenue
cost_structure.profit: 2022: profit was $27.0 million, equal to 3.7% of revenue
cost_structure.margin_pressure: 2025: fixed-price public bids and long lead times make margins sensitive to chassis price increases, steel volatility, tariffs, labor shortages and supplier delays
cost_structure.capital_intensity: 2022: low capital intensity in the baseline because final-stage assembly relies heavily on skilled labor and purchased vehicle platforms rather than fully automated mass production

major_players: REV Group Inc. ambulance brands including AEV, Horton, Leader, Road Rescue and Wheeled Coach
J.B. Poindexter & Co. / Demers Braun Crestline Medix, including Demers, Braun, Crestline and Medix
American Response Vehicles and regional final-stage builders
current_dynamics: 2025-2026 demand is less about new market creation and more about replacement cycles catching up. EMS agencies delayed purchases during chassis and component shortages, then faced 24-month-plus lead times and sharply higher unit prices. Public agencies are ordering earlier, using remounts to extend patient modules, and prioritizing reliability, serviceability and compliance. REV’s fiscal 2025 specialty-vehicle segment, which includes ambulances and fire apparatus, reported $1.8148 billion in net sales, up 5.1% from fiscal 2024, and cited increased fire and ambulance shipments, favorable ambulance mix and price realization. The segment’s fiscal 2025 backlog reached $4.4023 billion, up from $4.1798 billion in fiscal 2024, reflecting continued demand and pricing actions across fire apparatus and ambulance units.
whats_growing: Replacement demand, remounts, medium-duty units, fleet-standardized procurement, telematics, remote diagnostics, antimicrobial and safer patient compartments, higher-spec Type I units, and dealer/service support are growing. Demand is also supported by 2025 Census data showing the US 65+ population at 64.6 million and by CMS projections that national health spending will grow 5.4% annually on average from 2025 to 2034.
whats_shrinking: Impulse fleet expansion, low-spec purchases, small agencies’ ability to buy new units outright, and exports are constrained. Buyers are substituting remounts or refurbishments for new vehicles where budgets cannot absorb 2025 prices and long lead times. Baseline trade data already showed 2022 exports at $44.9 million after a 2017-2022 annualized decline, and high domestic backlogs make export growth less attractive for many US builders.
recent_developments: 2025-04-03: Coalinga, California staff reported new ambulance build lead times had increased to a 24-month minimum and cited a 2025 new ambulance cost expectation of about $445,000.
2025-06-04: REV Group reported fiscal Q2 2025 specialty-vehicle backlog of $4.2820 billion, up from $4.0644 billion in fiscal Q2 2024, with demand from fire apparatus and ambulance units.
2025-06-26: J.B. Poindexter announced the acquisition of Demers Braun Crestline Medix, adding a North American ambulance portfolio with more than 70,000 units delivered globally.
2025-12-09: REV Group reported fiscal 2025 specialty-vehicle backlog of $4.4023 billion, up from $4.1798 billion in fiscal 2024, citing continued fire and ambulance demand and pricing actions.
2026-03-10: CMS posted CY 2026 Ambulance Fee Schedule files and noted temporary ground ambulance add-on payments extended through December 31, 2027.
2026-06-01: NTEA highlighted its Ambulance Manufacturers Division work on emergency-vehicle safety, research, standards and industry collaboration.
outlook: The industry outlook is stable but capacity-constrained. The baseline forecast called for 2027 revenue of $708.9 million in 2022 dollars, but 2025-2026 public evidence suggests nominal revenue is being supported by price realization, long backlogs and overdue fleet replacement. Unit growth should remain modest because municipal budgets, reimbursement pressure and chassis availability cap conversion speed. Remounting will keep growing as a budget and lead-time workaround, while consolidation gives REV and J.B. Poindexter scale advantages in purchasing, dealer coverage, engineering and compliance. Over the 2026-2028 period, the biggest upside is faster chassis normalization and federal/local funding for EMS fleets; the biggest downside is another input-cost spike or public-budget slowdown.
themes: Aging population and higher EMS utilization
Chassis supply and final-stage manufacturing bottlenecks
Consolidation among North American ambulance brands
Public procurement and Medicare reimbursement exposure
Price realization versus municipal budget pressure

title: Animal Food Production in the US
one_liner: A mature, scale-driven manufacturing industry balancing steady livestock-feed demand with higher-margin pet-food growth.
overview: The industry converts grains, oilseeds, rendered proteins, vitamins, minerals and specialty ingredients into livestock feed, poultry feed, cattle feed, swine feed, dog food, cat food and other animal diets. The 2022 IBISWorld baseline described a $68.4 billion industry growing 1.5% in 2022, with dog food, cat food, poultry feed and cattle feed as the core revenue pools. Current 2025-2026 data point to a split market: pet food and treats continue to grow at retail, while total NAICS 3111 animal-food manufacturing output is flatter because livestock-feed volumes are tied to herd and flock cycles and commodity-price pass-through.

key_stats.market_size: Estimated $72.5 billion in 2025 US animal food manufacturing output, based on BLS/FRED 2024 sectoral output of $72.661 billion adjusted by 2025 real sectoral output and 2025 animal-food PPI.
key_stats.growth: Estimated -0.2% nominal growth in 2025 versus 2024 using BLS/FRED real output and PPI data.
key_stats.latest_official_output: BLS/FRED sectoral output for NAICS 3111 was $72.661 billion in 2024, down from $77.306 billion in 2023 and up from $72.884 billion in 2022.
key_stats.real_output: BLS/FRED real sectoral output index was 101.299 in 2025 versus 102.500 in 2024 and 99.407 in 2022.
key_stats.production_index: Federal Reserve/FRED industrial production for NAICS 3111 was 93.9056 in 2025 versus 93.1368 in 2024 and 98.3608 in 2022, indexed to 2017=100.
key_stats.producer_prices: BLS/FRED animal-food manufacturing PPI averaged 208.899 in 2025 versus 206.877 in 2024; May 2026 was 218.465.
key_stats.pet_food_retail: APPA reported US pet food and treats sales of $68.3 billion in 2025 and projected $69.7 billion for 2026.
key_stats.pet_ownership: APPA reported 95 million US households owned at least one pet in 2025.
key_stats.economic_footprint: AFIA reported a $267.1 billion animal-food industry economic footprint for fiscal 2024-2025.

baseline_2022.market_size: $68.409 billion revenue in 2022, per IBISWorld baseline file.
baseline_2022.growth: 1.5% revenue growth in 2022, per IBISWorld baseline file.
baseline_2022.profit: $3.352 billion profit in 2022, with a 4.9% profit margin.
baseline_2022.exports: $4.671 billion exports in 2022, equal to 6.8% of 2022 revenue.
baseline_2022.imports: $3.344 billion imports in 2022, equal to 5.0% of 2022 domestic demand.
baseline_2022.product_mix: Dog food was 33.3% of 2022 revenue, cat food 12.5%, poultry feed 19.5%, cattle feed 17.3% and pig feed 7.8%.

how_it_makes_money: Producers sell bagged, bulk and contract-manufactured animal diets to farms, integrators, farm-supply wholesalers, pet retailers, mass merchants, grocery channels, e-commerce platforms and veterinarians. Livestock-feed revenue is driven by feed tonnage, species mix and grain/oilseed cost pass-through, while pet-food revenue benefits from brands, premium formulations, therapeutic diets, fresh and refrigerated formats, treats and subscription or online channels.
cost_structure: The 2022 cost base was dominated by purchases of corn, soymeal, oilseeds, rendered proteins, meat byproducts, vitamins, minerals, packaging and freight; wages were $3.968 billion in 2022 and profit was 4.9% of revenue. In 2025-2026, lower corn and soybean-meal costs helped livestock-feed margins, while 2026 animal-food PPI gains show renewed price pressure after a flat 2025 pricing environment. Pet-food manufacturers also carry higher marketing, quality-control, food-safety and formulation costs because premium and therapeutic products rely on brand trust and regulatory compliance.
major_players: CHS animal nutrition and feed businesses
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 industry is being pulled in two directions. Pet food remains the higher-growth and higher-margin side, with APPA reporting $68.3 billion of US pet food and treat retail sales in 2025 and a $69.7 billion 2026 projection. Total animal-food manufacturing is less buoyant because BLS/FRED real sectoral output fell from 102.500 in 2024 to 101.299 in 2025, while industrial production remained below its 2022 level. Feed demand is supported by poultry, dairy, cattle and hog production, but producer revenue is sensitive to corn, soybean meal, freight and livestock cycles.
whats_growing: Premium pet diets, cat food, wet food, fresh and refrigerated formats, therapeutic and science-backed products, online pet-food purchasing, upcycled pet-food ingredients and large-scale feed automation are growing in 2025-2026. APPA reported pet food and treats rising from $66.0 billion in 2024 to $68.3 billion in 2025, and PFI/IFEEDER reported $51.7 billion of 2024 dog and cat food sales supported by 9.8 million tons of production.
whats_shrinking: Real animal-food manufacturing output shrank 1.2% in 2025 versus 2024, and BLS/FRED nominal sectoral output declined from $77.306 billion in 2023 to $72.661 billion in 2024 before the estimated flat 2025 result. Commodity-price pass-through is also less supportive than during the 2021-2023 inflation spike, and some value-oriented pet-food and livestock-feed buyers are trading down or resisting price increases in 2025-2026.
recent_developments: 2025-04: PFI and IFEEDER reported $51.7 billion of 2024 US dog and cat food sales and 9.8 million tons of 2024 pet-food production.
2025-08: PetfoodIndustry listed 2024 US pet-food company revenues, led by Nestle Purina at $22.457 billion and Mars Petcare at $22.000 billion.
2025-09: AFIA reported a $267.1 billion fiscal 2024-2025 economic footprint for the US animal-food industry.
2026-03: APPA reported US pet industry sales of $158 billion in 2025 and projected $165 billion for 2026.
2026-06: BLS/FRED reported 2025 NAICS 3111 real sectoral output of 101.299, down from 102.500 in 2024.
2026-06: BLS/FRED reported animal-food manufacturing PPI at 218.465 in May 2026, up from the 2025 average of 208.899.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is stable but not fast-growing. Pet food should keep expanding because APPA projects pet food and treats at $69.7 billion in 2026, supported by 95 million pet-owning households in 2025 and continued demand for premium and health-oriented products. Livestock feed should remain volume-dependent, with USDA 2026 feed-grain outlooks pointing to ample grain supplies but continued sensitivity to weather, export demand and soybean crush. Margins should benefit when corn and soybean-meal prices stay moderate, but 2026 PPI increases suggest producers may again face cost recovery challenges.
themes: Low-concentration manufacturing base with concentrated branded pet food leaders
one_sentence: Animal Food Production in the US manufactures feed for livestock and food for pets, with 2025 revenue estimated at $72.5 billion as pet food keeps expanding while real animal-food output remains below its 2022 level.
